taxa.grankReasons: Vitis acerifolia is a woody vine native to the southern Great Plains in the United States, occurring from Colorado south to Texas and east to western Oklahoma and Kansas. It is locally uncommon in eastern New Mexico. Vitis acerifolia is considered a valuable wild relative of the cultivated wine grape (V. vinifera) due to its potential as rootstock, resistance to pathogens, and tolerance to salt, drought, and boron. Specific threats to Vitis acerifolia are not well documented; however, the areas in which it occurs are threatened by habitat loss and degradation.

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis acerifolia is native to the southern Great Plains in the United States, where it locally common. Its range extends from eastern Colorado and New Mexico, through northern Texas to western Kansas and Oklahoma (Flora of North America 2016). The range extent is estimated to be 587,500 square kilometers. Occurrences beyond North America are not native and not included in Range Extent Calculations. Two specimens, one collected in Coahuila, Mexico and another recorded from Fresno, California are cultivated and originate from the US Department of Agriculture National Plant Germplasm System (USDA ARS 2021). According to Jepson (2021), this species does not occur in California. There is one record of Vitis acerifolia from Louisiana that is misidentified (J. Wen pers. comm. 2021).
rankInfo.popSizeComments: Vitis acerifolia is locally common in the Great Plains and uncommon in New Mexico.
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Although Vitis acerifolia is locally common in the Great Plains, it is threatened by herbicide use along highways by state departments of transportation (Walker et al 2019). Vitis acerifolia is likely threatened by habitat loss, invasive species, grazing, drought, and other widespread threats; however, declines to this species are not well documented.

plantCharacteristics.economicComments: Vitis acerifolia is considered a tertiary gene pool to the cultivated grape, Vitis vinifera (Khoury 2013; USDA ARS 2021). It has traits valuable for use in rootstock breeding, such as drought resistance (Padgett-Johnson et al. 2003). It can exclude chloride ions and has some resistance to boron, important traits for rootstock (Heinitz et al. 2019; Walker et al. 2019). It has some resistance to powdery mildew (Fayyaz et al. 2021) and to root-knot nematodes (USDA ARS 2004). It is one of the parents of Vitis x doaniana, an economically valuable natural hybrid used for rootstock improvement (USDA ARS 2004). Callen et al. (2016) suggested that Vitis acerifolia, a close relative of the rootstock sources V. riparia and V. rupestris, might be considered as a novel source of rootstock as vineyards are affected by climate change. It roots easily from dormant cuttings (Walker et al. 2019).

plantCharacteristics.economicComments:
Vitis arizonica is used by several Native American groups, and is known to have been cultivated. The fruit is edible and can be eaten fresh, dried, or used as vinegar (Riordan and Nabhan 2019).

Vitis arizonica is considered a tertiary gene pool to the cultivated grape, V. vinifera (Khoury 2013; USDA ARS 2021). It is used in breeding to improve pest and pathogen resistance in the cultivated grape. For example, it is resistant to the dagger nematode, which feeds on grape rootstock and is a vector for viral disease (Walker et al. 2017). It confers resistance to Pierce's Disease, a bacterium that causes significant damage to wine grapes (Morales-Cruz 2021; Riaz 2020). Vitis arizonica is also able to tolerate drought and boron, important characteristics for rootstock (Padgett-Johnson et al. 2003; Walker et al. 2017).

If V. berlandieri's current range is limited to Texas and northern Mexico along the border, it is likely more imperiled than the current rank of G4, Apparently Secure. rankInfo.rangeExtentComments:
Vitis berlandieri occurs in Texas, United States and in several states in Mexico (Flora of North America 2016). In Texas, V. berlandieri occurs from Fort Davis in the west to the Brazos River in the east, mostly found in the Edwards Plateau and most abundant in the Hill Country west of Austin (Walker et al. 2019). One study reported V. berlandieri from Arkansas, United States, but this has not been confirmed by the floristic literature or herbarium specimens.

According to a checklist of Mexican vascular plants, Vitis berlandieri has been reported from 14 states: Coahuila, Colima, Durango, Hidalgo, Jalisco, Michoacán, Nayarit, Nuevo León, Puebla, Querétaro, San Luis Potosí, Tamaulipas, Veracruz, and Zacatecas (Villaseñor 2016). Flora of North America indicates that V. berlandieri occurs in the states of Coahuila, Nuevo León, and Tamaulipas while Ibarra-Manriquez et al. (2015) lists Durango, Jalisco, Michoacán, and Tamaulipas. However, Walker et al. (2019) indicate a smaller current range for V. berlandieri, mostly confined to the Edwards Plateau in central Texas. Walker et al. (2019) report that V. berlandieri is also found in northern Mexico, although these populations are diminishing from threats such as overgrazing and rerouting of water sources.

To calculate the extent of occurrence, localities from Oklahoma, United States and Baja California and Chihuahua, Mexico were removed. Localities reported from Mexico within the states listed by Villaseñor (2016) were included in the calculation. The resulting extent of occurrence is estimated to be 1.1-1.2 million square kilometers.
rankInfo.numberEosComments: Although the number of element occurrences has not been calculated for V. berlandieri, it is known from over 200 herbarium specimens in the United States and Mexico (GBIF 2023).
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Vitis berlandieri is threatened in the eastern part of its Texas range by deer grazing, agriculture, and residential development of the Texas Hill Country (Walker et al. 2019, Uretsky 2018). In this region, large ranches have been broken up into small lots and homeowners eradicate vines from their properties (Walker et al. 2019). Populations in Mexico are threatened by changing hydrology due to water diversions along the Rio Grande River (Walker et al 2019).
rankInfo.enviromentalSpecificityComments: The species is found in a narrow ecological niche in the Edwards Plateau region (Uretsky 2018).

plantCharacteristics.economicComments: Vitis berlandieri is considered a tertiary crop wild relative of the cultivated grape, V. vinifera (USDA ARS 2022 as syn. V. cinerea var. helleri). Vitis berlandieri is one the primary sources of rootstock for cultivated grapevines globally. It is most well-known for its role as one of three North American species that reestablished the European wine industry in the late 1800s, when many vineyards were decimated by the introduced phylloxera pest (Heinitz et al. 2019). The ability of V. berlandieri to grow in calcareous soils is an important trait for many European vineyards with similar soil types. However, because V. berlandieri does not root easily from cuttings, it is often bred with other Vitis rootstock sources, particularly V. riparia and V. rupestris (Uretsky 2018). Vitis berlandieri is also known for being tolerant of drought and high levels of potassium (Schmid et al. 2006, Uretsky 2018).

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis californica occurs in California and Oregon in the United States. Flora of North America (2016) indicates that the native range of V. californica comprises central and northern California, extending north from San Luis Obispo and Inyo counties to southern Oregon. Dangl et al. (2015) include the Tehachapi Mountains as part of the native range, which occur in Kern and Los Angeles counties. Citizen science observations of this species have been recorded from further south in California (e.g., San Diego County) and in Mexico near the San Diego border (Tijuana). However, identification of this species is difficult due to extensive hybridization with the native V. girdiana and introduced V. vinifera. Therefore, observations of V. californica south of Los Angeles county are not included within this assessment of the native range until observations can be verified.
rankInfo.numberEosComments: There are over 500 specimen-based localities in the Global Biodiversity Information Facility but it is unclear how many Element Occurrences there are, especially due to widespread hybridization of V. californica with V. vinifera.
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Vitis californica is threatened by frequent hybridization with the non-native grapevine, V. vinifera. Walker et al. (2019) describe V. californica as "almost extinct" in California due to the threat of hybridization. Southwestern Vitis species are threatened by grazing, drought, invasive species, and herbicide use along highways (Fayyaz et al. 2021, Heinitz et al 2019).
rankInfo.intrinsicVulnerabilityComments: Vitis californica tends toward clonal propagation in its natural habitat. Clonal populations form extensive woody vines that shade the understory, inhibiting seedling germination and establishment (Dangl et al. 2015). In addition, natural recruitment can be severely limited due to a smaller ratio of female to male vines in the population. In combination, these factors can significantly limit natural recruitment, which may result in inbreeding (Dangl et al. 2015).

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis cinerea occurs in eastern North America, where it is common along moist, lowland habitats along the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers (Flora of North America 2016, Weakley et al. 2022, Moore 1991). The distribution of V. cinerea is uncertain, with sometimes conflicting information along the outer extent of the species' range. Occurrences from Wisconsin, Florida, and Virginia should be examined since they are beyond the range given by Flora of North America (2016, as syn. V. cinerea var. cinerea). Moore (1991) excludes Wisconsin and Virginia from the range, but includes the Florida panhandle. Even with this uncertainty, the calculated range extent for this species is likely at least 1 million square kilometers.
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Much of eastern North America's forested habitats have, and continue to be, impacted by development. While this has likely impacted populations of V. cinerea, the species seems to be able to reestablish after disturbance. Vitis cinerea is also likely threatened by habitat loss, invasive species, and other widespread threats; however, declines to this species are not well documented.

Vitis labrusca hybridizes with V. riparia, resulting in Vitis x novae-angliae (Walker et al. 2019).
taxa.grankReasons: Vitis labrusca is a high-climbing vine that occurs throughout much of eastern North America. It occurs in a variety of habitats, primarily in areas that are moist to wet. Although its habitat has been impacted by threats, V. labrusca remains a widespread species. Vitis labrusca hybridizes with the cultivated wine grape (V. vinifera); cultivated hybrids such as 'Concord' continue to be used in the production of table grapes, jelly, and sweet wine. Some hybrids of V. labrusca have escaped cultivation and become naturalized in areas of North America outside of its native range.

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis labrusca is native to the eastern part of North America, occurring as far north as Ontario, Canada, and south to Georgia in the United States (Flora of North America 2016). The species is cultivated and has escaped cultivation in several regions of the continent, including the Pacific Northwest, the northeastern part of Canada (New Brunswick, Nova Scotia), southern California, and parts of the Midwest (e.g., Missouri). Flora of North America (2016) lists the following province and states as the native range of V. labrusca (ON, AL, CT, DE, DC, GA, IL, IN, KY, ME, MD, MA, MI, MS, NH, NJ, NY, NC, OH, PA, RI, SC, TN, VT, VA, WI). Herbarium specimens outside of the native range included in Flora of North America (2016) were not included in calculating the Extent of Occurrence. Specimens in Illinois may also be introduced; however, the rating assigned for the Extent of Occurrence would not change with the removal of locality data from Illinois.
rankInfo.numberEosComments: Vitis labrusca is known from over 500 herbarium specimens and has a wide geographic distribution in the eastern part of North America. Therefore, there are inferred to be greater than 300 element occurrences.
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Specific threats to V. labrusca are not well-documented. The habitat in which it occurs has been affected by development, agriculture, invasive species, and other threats common to eastern North America. However, since V. labrusca can occupy disturbed habitats, it is not possible to calculate the scope or severity of threats to this species.

plantCharacteristics.economicComments: Vitis labrusca is considered a tertiary crop wild relative of the cultivated grape, V. vinifera (USDA ARS 2021, Khoury 2013). Vitis labrusca hybridizes with V. vinifera, which was present in North America as a result of repeated attempts at cultivation by European immigrants. While V. labrusca and V. vinifera are able to hybridize in the wild, hybrids are also intentionally selected and cultivated. These hybrids are often referred to as Vitis x labruscana (Walker et al. 2019), and they formed the beginning of the grape industry in the eastern United States (Hedrick et al. 1908). The most well-known and commercially important of these hybrids are ‘Catawba’ and ‘Concord’ (Huber et al. 2016), which were brought into cultivation in the 1800s. To this day, the hybrid cultivars of V. labrusca and V. vinifera, especially the 'Concord' grape, are used to produce table grapes, juice, jelly, and sweet wine (Heinitz et al. 2019). The "foxy" flavor (methyl anthranilate) of V. labrusca grapes has limited their use in the wine industry (Heinitz et al. 2019). As a crop wild relative of the wine grape, V. labrusca has shown some evidence of resistance to the following diseases of grape: powdery and downy mildew, anthracnose, and Flavesence doree (Heinitz et al. 2019).

taxa.grankReasons: Vitis monticola is a climbing vine that is endemic to the Edwards Plateau in Texas, United States. It is restricted to a narrow range occupying well-drained soils. Specific threats and trends are not well-documented for this species; however, its habitat has been affected by grazing, non-native invasive species, increased herbicide use, and changes in canopy structure. Vitis monticola is used as rootstock for the wine grape (V. vinifera). It is also considered part of the tertiary genepool to the wine grape. As the most drought-tolerant grape species native to North America, V. monticola may contain germplasm important for increased drought tolerance in the wine grape.

taxa.taxonomicComments: Flora of North America (2016) does not recognize varieties or subspecies of Vitis riparia. Specifically, plants recognized as V. riparia var. syrticola (found on dunes around the Great Lakes, see Catling and Mitrow 2005) were found to be synonymous with V. riparia because the variation in leaf hairiness is continuous rather than distinct (Flora of North America 2016). Additional varieties and subspecies have been recognized in the past, including var. praecox, but none are considered distinct by Flora of North America (2016) and most local floras. Vitis riparia naturally hybridizes with other Vitis species and is thought to be one of the parents of of Vitis x novae-angliae with V. labrusca (Flora of North America 2016, Wen et al. 2018).
taxa.grankReasons: Vitis riparia is a woody vine that is native throughout much of North America, ranging from Canada south to Texas and from the Rocky Mountains east to the Atlantic Coast. It has become naturalized in Saskatchewan (Canada) and in Oregon and Washington (United States). Vitis riparia is particularly important to the cultivated grapevine (V. vinifera) because it is one of three North American species that reestablished the European wine industry in the late 1800s, when many vineyards were decimated by the introduced phylloxera pest. To this day,Vitis riparia is still one of the primary sources of rootstock in grape production worldwide. Vitis riparia is a very wide-ranging species that occurs in many different habitats. While it is likely affected by several different threats, Vitis riparia is so widespread that it is considered to be at a very low risk of extinction.

Vitis riparia is considered native in most of its range; however, it is not native and has become naturalized in Saskatchewan, Canada and in Oregon and Washington in the United States (Flora of North America 2016). The range extent was calculated using localities only within the native range.
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Vitis riparia is a wide-ranging species that occurs in many different habitats. While this species is likely affected by several different threats, including development and invasive species, there is limited information available to estimate the scope and severity of each threat. There are likely more impacts of threats on the edges of its range, particularly invasive vines. In the drier parts of its range, changes in hydrology are affecting Vitis riparia. Other threats affecting this species include deforestation, cattle grazing along riparian zones, and herbicide drift from agricultural fields. Vitis riparia is also mistakenly removed from areas because it resembles non-native invasive vines, particularly porcelain berry (Ampelopsis glandulosus).

taxa.taxonomicComments: There are two commonly recognized subgenera in the Grape Family (Vitaceae). The subgenus Vitis, includes the majority of species in the family. The subgenus Muscadinia includes two species: Vitis rotundifolia, including its varieties, and Vitis popenei (Flora of North America 2016). Some authors (e.g., Weakley et al. 2020) elevate subgenus Muscadinia to the rank of genus (Wen et al. 2018). Subgenus Muscadinia differs from subgenus Vitis in having simple tendrils, larger fruits, seeds with longer ventral infolds, and 40 chromosomes rather than 38 (Wen et al. 2018).

plantCharacteristics.economicComments: Vitis rotundifolia, the muscadine grape, is both a crop and a crop wild relative. Muscadine grapes, including cultivated varieties like Scuppernong, are eaten as fresh fruit and used to make wines and jellies. Vitis rotundifolia is a tertiary crop wild relative to the cultivated grape, Vitis vinifera (Khoury 2013; USDA ARS 2021). Muscadine grapes are resistant to many diseases that affect Vitis vinifera cultivars including Pierce's Disease, grapevine downy mildew, and powdery mildew (Buck and Worthington 2022). Due to this disease resistance, germplasm from the muscadine grape has been used to improve varieties of the cultivated grape. However, muscadine grapes are difficult to cross with cultivated grapes due to different numbers of chromosomes (muscadine grapes have 40 chromosomes while the cultivated grape has 38 chromosomes, Walker et al. 2019). While Vitis rotundifolia has been used to improve V. vinifera cultivars, the number of utilized V. rotundifolia genotypes is limited and only represents a small portion of the full genetic diversity within V. rotundifolia (Buck and Worthington 2022). In addition, the germplasm originally used for breeding muscadine grapes was limited to a relatively small part of the species' native range, primarily from the coastal plains of North Carolina (Buck and Worthington 2022). Vitis rotundifolia has much more potential to be utilized as both a crop and crop wild relative to improve cultivated grapevines.

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments:
Vitis rufotomentosa is known from the southeastern United States; however, its distribution is unclear. Small (1903) described the range of V. rufotomentosa as from "Florida to Louisiana," whereas Weakley et al. (2023) described the range of V. rufotomentosa as endemic to the southeastern U.S., occurring from Florida to North Carolina "and perhaps more widespread." Determining the range of Vitis rufotomentosa will require reviewing herbarium specimens currently identified as V. aestivalis or possibly other Vitis species.

Vitis rufotomentosa is documented from Florida, North Carolina, and possibly Louisiana and Texas. A primary part of the species' range is in Florida, where it is considered uncommon in the south and rare in the north (Weakley et al. 2023). Vitis rufotomentosa is documented from two North Carolina localities: an herbarium specimen collected in 2023 from Wilson County, and an iNaturalist record observed in 2022 from the Uhwarrie National Forest in Montgomery County. The species is known from a single specimen in Louisiana, collected from Kisatchie in 1947. Three specimens of V. rufotomentosa from Texas would likely be considered V. lincecumii based on Weakley et al. (2023), but should be reviewed.
rankInfo.numberEosComments: The exact number of occurrences is unknown, but is estimated to be between 6 and 300. While there are currently fewer than 20 herbarium specimens (GBIF 2024), the number of specimens and occurrences is likely to increase once specimens are updated to reflect the change in taxonomy elevating V. rufotomentosa to species level from a variety of V. aestivalis.

plantCharacteristics.economicComments: Vitis rufotomentosa is assumed to be a tertiary crop wild relative of the cultivated grape, Vitis vinifera, based on crop wild relative classifications for closely related North American native Vitis species (USDA ARS 2023). This species is a source of resistance to the dagger nematode (Xiphinema index) that feeds on the root tips of the cultivated grapevine (V. vinifera) and transmits the grapevine fanleaf virus (Reisch et al. 2012, Walker et al. 2019). For this reason, V. rufotomentosa is used in breeding to develop rootstocks for the cultivated grapevine.

taxa.grankReasons: Vitis rupestris is a shrubby perennial grape that occurs sporadically across a fairly broad range in the eastern United State where it is restricted to river scour and stream banks with some affinity to calcareous regions. The species is primarily threatened the alteration of natural flood regimes that maintain a favorable successional state for the species. It is especially vulnerable due to intrinsic vulnerabilities (low rate of seed production) and slow vegetative spread as a clonal species, and low genetic diversity within populations, with few genotypes represented even in large stands. Colonization of new sites is rare due to these limitations and the specific habitat requirements. Vitis rupestris is particularly important to the cultivated grapevine (V. vinifera) because it is one of three North American species that reestablished the European wine industry in the late 1800s, when many vineyards were decimated by the introduced phylloxera pest. Vitis rupestris is still used as rootstock in grape production worldwide for its resistance to phylloxera, downy mildew, and other fungal diseases affecting the wine and grape industries. Interestingly, this species has escaped and naturalized in both Europe and California, despite its rarity in the eastern United States.

Reports from Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, and Ohio are based on old literature reports not maintained in more recent floras. The Ohio report appears to be without basis (A. rankInfo.numberEosComments: There are between 100 and 130 occurrences rangewide. In addition, there are nearly 50 occurrences not seen for over 40 years (iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023, SEINet 2023).
rankInfo.popSizeComments: This species is locally common in Missouri, where it is known from most counties in the Ozark region (Kutz 1997). Abundance is difficult to estimate; however, because V. rupestris grows in thickets and reproduces vegetatively. Both physical and genetic individuals are difficult to tell apart. In Arkansas, threats to the species are low and it is stable, but there are less than 250 plants (B. Baker, pers. comm. 2020).
rankInfo.viabilityComments: Of the occurrences where viability has been assessed, there are 15 occurrences with good viability.
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: The principal threat to Vitis rupestris is a change in the hydrology of its riverbank habitats, away from the natural flooding regime and periodic scouring of the riverbank. Riverbanks and hydrology have been altered by dams, roads, powerplants, and other forms of development. The species relies on a natural flooding regime and periodic scouring of the riverbank to maintain its habitat but these alterations can increase or diminish flood intensity and frequency to a level that is not favorable by the species. Changes to hydrology may be exacerbated by climate change. This species is also threatened by succession which is also maintained by flooding and scouring. Its habitat may be threatened by recreational use and by pollution or siltation. Deer browse of plants is evident at some sites. Hybridization with other native grapes may be degrading this species' gene pool (S. Grund, pers. comm., 2022).
rankInfo.shortTermTrendComments: This species is apparently declining throughout much of its range (Jun Wen, pers. comm. 2023), although probably stable in the Ozarks (Tim Smith, pers. comm. 2001).
rankInfo.longTermTrendComments: There are nearly 50 occurrences not seen for over 40 years (iNaturalist 2023, NatureServe 2023, SEINet 2023).
rankInfo.inventoryNeeds: Determining the status of Vitis rupestris throughout its range, both in areas where it is more common and where it is more rare are urgently needed. Anecdotal information suggests a decline in the mid-Atlantic area but this has yet to be formally documented. Additional surveys of suitable habitat are needed to identify previously undocumented occurrences.
rankInfo.numberProtEosComments: Vitis rupestris occurs on protected lands in Indiana (Crawford State Park), Kentucky (Cane Creek Wildlife Management Area, Daniel Boone National Forest, Kentucky Ridge State Forest, Pine Mountain State Park Nature Preserve, Memorial Nature Preserve), Pennsylvania (Ohiopyle State Park), Tennessee (Rock Island State Park), Virginia (Harper's Ferry National Historic Park, George Washington and Jefferson National Forest, Goshen Pass Natural Area, Great Falls National Park), and West Virginia (New River Gorge National River, Pipestem State Park, Valley Falls State Park). This species is a U.S. Forest Service Region 9 Sensitive Species. While this species may occur on public or protected lands, impacts to hydrological regimes can occur far from occurrences.
rankInfo.protectionNeeds: Sites recommended for in situ protection by Pavek and colleagues should be formally protected and managed.
rankInfo.intrinsicVulnerabilityComments: Vitis rupestris populations are persistent if the natural flood regime maintained; however, the species will not persist in areas with altered hydrology due to the ensuing changes in habitat. Since it spreads vegetatively as a clonal shrub (not as a vine), sizable stands may have only one or a few genotypes represented. The low rate of seed production and the narrow habitat requirements makes establishment of new occurrences of this species infrequent.

Vitis rupestris is still one of the primary sources of rootstock in grape production worldwide, used for its resistance to phylloxera, downy mildew, and other fungal diseases that plague the wine and grape industries (Arrigo and Arnold 2007, Best et al. 1996, Heinitz et al. 2019).

elementManagement.stewardshipOverview: Continue to monitor known populations for status of threats, site condition, and abundance of plants. Survey potential habitat for new populations. Seek long term protection for exceptional sites. Review most critical threats and consider the feasibility of their removal/control and how those efforts will impact the quality of habitat for the species, as well as other species of interest. Record and monitor the impact of management actions that are directed towards the species or habitat. Maintain the hydrology of habitats for this species, especially the periodic riverbank cycle of flooding and scouring. Also, invasive and exotic plant species should be removed from the habitat.

elementManagement.siteConservationPlansConsidered: Preserve design should include adequate buffer area surrounding occurrences to allow for management activities. These include habitat where stream scouring can occur and will not be altered by changes in hydrology (dams) in the foreseeable future. Contact Water Resource Agencies to acknowledge the presence of this element in their district as a protection against channelization or impoundment of the site. A 100 ft riparian buffer zone is also suggested (Concannon, J., 1996).

elementManagement.managementResearchPrograms: Seeds are viable and can be germinated if placed in sand and held near freezing for one month (Moore, M., 1996).
elementManagement.biologicalResearchNeeds: Research needs include determining reasons for this species' decline, documenting the genetic diversity of the species throughout its range, and resolving conflicting information on its status as a calciphile. speciesCharacteristics.reproductionComments: Reproduction is mainly vegetative via rooting stems, although plants do flower and produce fruit. Germination rates are improved with chilling at 4°C for 4 weeks (Takeno et al. 1983).
speciesCharacteristics.ecologyComments: Plant species associated with Vitis rupestris include Andropogon gerardii, Apocynum sp., Baptisia australis, Cornus obliqua, Platanus occidentalis, Salix caroliniana, and Ulmus alata (Morano and Walker 1995). In Indiana, V. rupestris occurs in chert and limestone gravel streambeds. The elevation of one site was noted as 430 ft. (Indiana Heritage files 1995). In Kentucky, occurrences of this species are among limestone cobble bars and scoured boulder areas (Kentucky Heritage Files 1995). In Missouri, Vitis rupestris occurs along cherty stream beds, rocky banks, and gravel bars. These sites are alternately xeric and inundated (Steyermark,1993). In Pennsylvania, Vitis rupestris occurs along river banks that are reached by high water.
speciesCharacteristics.habitatComments: Vitis rupestris occurs on calcareous or gravelly banks, river bottoms, stream beds, washes, and scoured boulders and cobbles. It also occurs along the edges of limestone glades and barrens.
speciesCharacteristics.generalDescription: Bushy shrub-like grape, slightly climbing with few tendrils, alternate, short, wide, and toothed leaves. Berries are black.
speciesCharacteristics.diagnosticCharacteristics: Tendrils lacking or only from the uppermost nodes; leaves pubescent underneath with short erect hairs not long cobweb-like hairs; pith interrupted by a diaphragm at each node.

taxa.grankReasons: Vitis shuttleworthii is a woody vine endemic to peninsular Florida, occurring in about 30 counties. It is threatened by continued habitat loss and development; however, it has a relatively large distribution and is known from many occurrences. It also tends to inhabit disturbed areas including fencerows. Vitis shuttleworthii is considered a valuable wild relative of the cultivated grape vine (V. vinifera) due to its resistance to a number of pests and diseases.

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis shuttleworthii is endemic to peninsular Florida in the United States. Previous records included West Indies as part of the distribution but recent sources list only Florida (Flora of North America 2016). There is one record reported from Alabama that was introduced through the nursery trade and not considered part of the species' native range.
rankInfo.numberEosComments: Vitis shuttleworthii occurs in 30 or more counties in Florida and there are more than 50 herbarium specimens.
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Much of Florida's woodland habitat has been converted to agricultural or grazing lands, or developed for housing, tourism, or industry. Threats to this species are considered low because it occurs in many protected areas throughout the state. It also occurs on woodland edges that are still abundant in many disturbed areas.
rankInfo.numberProtEosComments: Vitis shuttleworthii occurs in many protected areas throughout Florida including Everglades National Park, Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, and many state and local parks. Pavek et al. (2001) proposed four natural areas to be designated as preserves for in situ conservation of this species. While the four proposed sites (Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, Jonathan Dickinson State Park, Myakka River State Park, and Hillsborough River State Park) are maintained as natural areas, the actual preserves for conservation of V. shuttleworthii were not established.

plantCharacteristics.economicComments: Vitis shuttleworthii is considered a tertiary gene pool to the cultivated grape, Vitis vinifera (Khoury 2013; GRIN 2020). Vitis shuttleworthii has valuable germplasm because of resistance to Pierce's disease, foliar fungal diseases (including anthracnose), and dagger nematodes (USDA ARS 2004; Heinitz et al. 2019). It has relatively large berries and has been used to produce fruiting hybrids (USDA ARS 2004).

speciesCharacteristics.habitatComments: Vitis shuttleworthii is found in woodland borders, well-drained pinelands, lowland woods, fencerows, and thickets (Moore 1991, Pavek et al. 2001, Flora of North America 2016). It primarily occurs in hardwood hammocks (i.e., hydric, maritime, mesic, prairie, and rockland) and is also found in pine rockland and river floodplain lake habitat (Gann et al. 2020). Vitis shuttleworthii seems to require an intermediate fire interval. Frequent burns or lack of fire entirely may eliminate populations (Pavek et al. 2001).

taxa.taxonomicComments:
Kartesz (1994) and FNA (2016) recognize four varieties in Vitis cinerea including Vitis cinerea var. floridana (Vitis simpsonii), Vitis cinerea var. baileyana (Vitis baileyana), Vitis cinerea var. cinerea (Vitis cinerea), and Vitis cinerea var. helleri (Vitis berlandieri). These varieties were recognized as species by Small (1933) and their elevated status is supported by recent research (Wen et al. 2018) and in the treatment by Weakley and Southeastern Flora Team (2022).

Vitis simpsonii was thought to intergrade with V. baileyana at the edge of the Piedmont along the fall line (Flora of North America 2016); however, Talavera et al. (2023) found no evidence of introgression between these two taxa.
taxa.grankReasons: Vitis simpsonii is a woody vine that occurs throughout the coastal plain of the southeastern United States. Vitis simpsonii is potentially threatened by development, changes in hydrology, invasive species, and other threats prominent in eastern North America. However, these threats are considered negligible given the species' broad range. Monitoring of existing populations is important to improve our understanding of this species since it is now considered a full species rather than a variety of Vitis cinerea (var. floridana). With a large range extent, over 80 occurrences, and no obvious intrinsic vulnerabilities, this species is considered Apparently Secure (G4).

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis simpsonii occurs in the coastal plain of the Southeastern and Mid-Atlantic regions of the United States, from Maryland south to Florida and west to Louisiana. Flora of North America (2016) indicates that V. simpsonii is native to Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Virginia. Range extent was estimated using herbarium specimen and photo-based observation data (GBIF 2023). Specimens collected in Missouri and Texas were not included in the range extent calculation because they are outside of the native range according to Flora of North America (2016). These collections should be reviewed as they may represent a range extension; however, the range extent with these collections would not exceed 2,500,000 square kilometers.
rankInfo.numberEosComments: Based on herbarium records and photo-based observations, there are likely between 81 and 300 occurrences rangewide (GBIF 2023).

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis vulpina is broadly distributed in the United States, extending north into Canada (Flora of North America 2016). In the United States, it occurs along the Atlantic Coast from Florida north to at least New York. Occurrences have been documented as far north as Quebec City in Canada, but these occurrences were not verified by Flora of North America (2016). Walker et al. (2019) describe the range as only reaching as far north as Pennsylvania and Missouri, while Flora of North America (2016) includes Ontario within the species' range. The western extent of Vitis vulpina is considered to be South Dakota, extending south to Texas (Flora of North America 2016). Regardless of differing descriptions of the species range limits, Vitis vulpina is a very wide-ranging species with a total range extent exceeding 2.5 million square kilometers.

taxa.taxonomicComments: Vitis x champinii is a natural hybrid with its parentage attributed to V. mustangensis and V. rupestris according to Flora of North America (2016). Zecca et al. (2023) indicate that the origin of the species is disputed and that V. monticola and V. berlandieri could also contribute to parentage of this hybrid.
taxa.grankReasons: Vitis x champinii is a naturally occurring hybrid species endemic to the Edwards Plateau, Texas, in the United States. It is known from a few occurrences and is threatened by development and grazing. It is an important species to the breeding of the cultivated grape (V. vinifera), used as rootstock due to its resistance to nematodes and tolerance of drought and salinity.
taxa.grankAdjustmentReasons: Vitis x champinii is a naturally occurring hybrid recognized in Flora of North America. Its conservation status was calculated as G2 but because it was determined to be a hybrid with no conservation value, the rank was adjusted to GNA.

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis x champinii occurs on or near the Edwards Plateau in Texas, United States (Flora of North America 2016, Zecca et al. 2023).
rankInfo.numberEosComments: The exact number of occurrences is unknown. The three most recent herbarium specimens were collected in the 1980s by Comeaux (GBIF 2023). There are three observations from the 2020s that need verification (GBIF 2023). There are a number of specimens by Moore from Georgia but these are from cultivated material (GBIF 2023). More research is needed to determine the number of occurrences for this species.
rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Vitis x champinii is threatened by "rapid development of the Texas Hill Country, intense herbivory from deer and cattle populations" (Heinitz 2019). More monitoring is needed to determine the scope and severity of threats to this species.
rankInfo.longTermTrendComments: Munson (1909) indicates this species was once abundant in some locations in Llano and Gillespie Counties in Texas. This may indicate a decline in in the species population based on the limited distribution in the 2020s.

plantCharacteristics.economicComments: Vitis x champinii is widely used as rootstock and in rootstock breeding for the cultivated grape (V. vinifera, USDA ARS 2023, Heinitz et al. 2019). As it is from the Edwards Plateau of Texas, it grows well on limestone soils, which is an important trait for rootstocks used in parts of Europe (Zecca et al. 2020). Vitis x champinii is used in the cultivars ‘Ramsey,’ ‘Harmony,’ ‘Dog Ridge,’ and ‘Freedom’ (Heinitz et al. 2019). Due to its rarity and its importance in breeding, Vitis x champinii is a priority for both in situ and ex situ conservation (Heinitz et al. 2019).

taxa.grankReasons: Vitis x doaniana is a woody vine that occurs in Texas and Oklahoma. It is a naturally occurring hybrid of V. acerifolia and V. mustangensis. rankInfo.threatImpactComments: Vitis x doaniana is threatened by development, agriculture, and cattle grazing (Zecca et al. 2020).

taxa.taxonomicComments: Vitis x novae-angliae is a naturally occurring hybrid that is sometimes treated as a species (Fernald 1917). Flora of North America (2016), Kartesz (1994), and Kartesz (1999) treat this taxon as a hybrid. The putative parent species were identified as Vitis labrusca and V. riparia by Moore (1991) and confirmed by Zecca et al. (2020).
taxa.grankReasons: Vitis x novae-angliae is a woody vine that is common in the northeast United States, extending into Ontario, Canada. It is a naturally occurring hybrid of Vitis labrusca and V. riparia.
taxa.grankAdjustmentReasons: Vitis x novae-angliae is a naturally occurring hybrid recognized in Flora of North America. Its conservation status was calculated as G3G4 but because it was determined to be a hybrid with no conservation value, the rank was adjusted to GNA.

rankInfo.rangeExtentComments: Vitis x novae-angliae is common in New England (Moore 1991) and is considered to be native from Ontario, Canada to the United States in Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania (Flora of North America 2016). Collections outside of this range in the United States are not confirmed to be Vitis x novae-angliae and therefore not included in calculations for Range Extent or Area of Occupancy. Vitis x novae-angliae has escaped from cultivation in Europe (Ardenghi et al. 2015).
rankInfo.numberEosComments: Based on herbarium collections there are likely over 30 occurrences rangewide (GBIF 2023). It was reported to grow abundantly in thickets along river banks (Bailey 1934) and common in the New England area (Moore 1991).
